annotations.text:
WHY THIS EXISTS

Reported 22 November, setting up a new hub from scratch in the living room. A reset Brilliant switch was added through Add > A switch on the wall: it blinked, That's the one, and the page said Added. Nothing else happened. Nothing asked whether it dims, whether it has a motion sensor to use, how much light is on it, or whether it is one of a pair of switches for the same light. Afterward there was no way to tell what the switch was called or where it had gone.

The Brilliant app asked all of that when a switch was set up, and a switch that has been reset has forgotten every answer. Without them a dimmer comes back as on and off, the motion sensor stays silent, and the far switch of a stairway pair works nothing.

TODAY -- FROM THE SHIPPED PANEL

app/src/Adding.vue, beat four. let_in() in brain/hub/bridge.py answers with no device, so the page has no room and no name to offer, and the hub's own sentence ("It is on the house now.") lands inside "It turned out to be ...".

Underneath, the add stops after the first step. The bridge joins the switch to the network and nothing more: the switch is not given the key it needs to take commands, its own models are not bound, it is not told to report presses, and the key that would let the house set it up later is handed to the screen and thrown away. So the switch is on the network but is not yet a light anybody can use, which is why there was nothing to name. That half is not visual and gets fixed whatever is picked here.

WHAT A SWITCH CAN BE TOLD TODAY

Every board assumes only what has been proven on a real switch, and says so where it can't.

Proven:
- Pairing with another switch for the same light: the far switch can be told which switch is its partner, and to pass each press along. Done by hand on the stairway pair in September.
- Dimming: giving a switch a working dimmer's whole setup makes it dim. The setting is read only when the switch starts, so the person restarts it (the tab at the bottom) once at the end.
- Presence: a switch can report somebody walking up to it once it is told to. The house, not the switch, decides what to do with that, so On / On then off is a routine the house runs.

Not known yet:
- Which single setting means dimmer. Until it is found, On and off only gives the switch a non-dimming switch's setup instead.
- Wattage. Nowhere to write it has been found. B is the only board that asks it; A and C leave it out until there is.

A -- ASKED IN WORDS, ONE QUESTION AT A TIME
NOT CHOSEN, 22 November. C was picked.

Five questions, in the order that matters: what it controls, whether the bulbs dim, whether there is another switch for the same light, what to do when someone walks in, then its room and name. Answers so far stay above the question as sentences you can change. The end repeats them, then asks for the restart.

FOR: nothing new to learn, every answer is one tap, and "I'm not sure" hands the bulb question to the house.
AGAINST: it asks people things they often don't know (do my bulbs dim?), and it asks about a pair of switches without any way to point at the other one.

B -- ONE PAGE, THE USUAL ANSWERS ALREADY IN
NOT CHOSEN, 22 November -- and not gone: C ends on B's page, and it is the switch's settings afterward.

Everything on one page as settings, each starting at the usual answer: dims, a light, just this one switch, on then off when someone walks in. Change what is wrong, Blink the light to check which one it is, Save, restart.

FOR: fastest for somebody who knows their wiring, and the same page can be the switch's settings later, so there is one place to learn.
AGAINST: a page of settings is the opposite of a conversation, and its defaults will be wrong in silence. It is the only board that asks for watts, which most people would have to guess, and nothing on the hub can use it yet.

C -- THE HOUSE TRIES IT ON THE LIGHT, YOU SAY WHAT YOU SAW
CHOSEN, 22 NOVEMBER.

The same five steps as A, but the questions are about what the person can see, not what they know. The house switches the light on to find out it controls one ("nothing came on" means it is the far switch of a pair). It dims it and asks whether it got dimmer, so nobody has to know their bulbs. It listens while you press the other switch for the same light, so a pair is made by touching it, the only way a person can point at a switch. Only walking in, room and name are asked in words. It ends on B's page, every row saying how it was found, which is also the switch's settings page later.

FOR: everything a person can't know is found out on the real thing while they stand next to it, which is where design/adding says setup happens. It's the only direction where pairing is something you do, not something you pick.
AGAINST: slower, and it needs the person by the light. "I can't see it from here" covers a wall screen in another room.

Added when it was picked: Did it get dimmer? has a fourth answer, It didn't change, because a freshly set-up switch sometimes reads its load type only after a restart. It asks for the tab, then dims again.

DECIDED 22 NOVEMBER 2026

C, ending on B's page. Built with the add underneath fixed: the bridge finishes a switch it lets in (its key, its controls, its announcements), and the hub keeps the switch's own key so it can be set up again later.

WHY THIS IS BEING REDRAWN

Reported 22 November, setting up a second switch in the living room house, this one on bulbs that can't dim. The house dimmed the light to half and back. The bulbs didn't change: many LED bulbs that can't dim ignore half and only react near the bottom, where they cut out. They didn't flicker or buzz either, so none of the answers fit but "It didn't change" -- and that one asked for the switch to be restarted with its tab, which reads as starting it over.

Two things are wrong. The test stops at half, which is exactly where a bulb that can't dim gives nothing away. And "It didn't change" guesses that the switch hasn't taken dimming yet. That only happens on a switch that was set to on and off before; a switch that was just started over dims from the start, so on the switch this flow mostly meets, the guess is wrong.

TODAY -- FROM THE SHIPPED PANEL

app/src/SwitchSetup.vue, step 2. The house sends full, half, full three times (show() in brain/hub/wallswitch.py). The four answers are the ones C was picked with. "It didn't change" opens the second board: pull the tab, push it back, Watch again -- in the middle of the setup, where the end page already asks for the one restart the switch needs.

A -- ONE SLOW LOOK, ALL THE WAY DOWN
CHOSEN, 22 NOVEMBER.

The house takes the light slowly from full to almost off and back, twice, about five seconds each way. That one look answers it for every kind of bulb: a dimmable one gets dimmer the whole way, one that can't dim stays bright and then cuts out near the bottom (or never changes at all), and a poor one flickers or buzzes on the way.

The answers are what was seen, in those words, and each is final: no answer sends anybody to the tab. "Nothing changed at all" sits under "stayed bright, then went off" because it means the same thing -- on and off only. The one restart stays where it already was, at the end, once.

Cost: one more second of watching than today. The house never learns whether it was the bulb or the switch's mode that didn't dim, and doesn't need to: either way the right answer is on and off, and it can be changed on the light later.

DECIDED 22 NOVEMBER 2026

A, as drawn. The house takes the light slowly to almost off and back, twice (show() in brain/hub/wallswitch.py); the four answers are the board's; no answer sends anybody to the tab, and the one restart stays on the end page. Pinned by app/tests/switchSetup.test.ts and app/e2e/switch-setup.spec.ts.

Why A over B and C: one look and one question, every answer final. B spent a second screen on the very bulbs the question exists for; C needed the screen and the light in view at once.

B -- HALF FIRST, THEN LOWER IF NOTHING CHANGED
NOT CHOSEN, 22 November. A was picked.

Today's first look, unchanged, so a dimmable bulb is still settled in one look at half. "It didn't change" no longer goes to the tab: it starts a second look, down to almost off, with three answers -- it got dimmer, it went off or flickered, still nothing -- and the last two mean on and off only.

Cost: a second screen for exactly the bulbs that can't dim, which is the case that went wrong; and "It didn't change" at half still reads like a fault before the second look explains it.

C -- YOU SLIDE IT DOWN YOURSELF
NOT CHOSEN, 22 November. A was picked.

The person drags a slider on the screen and the light follows their finger, at their pace, stopping where they like. Then the same three answers as A.

Cost: it asks them to do the test rather than watch it, which needs the screen and the light in view at once -- true on a phone at the switch, often not on the wall. And a slow hand at the bottom is what shows a bulb that can't dim; a quick one can miss it.

WHY THIS IS BEING REDRAWN

Said 22 November, after setting up two switches: a light whose bulbs can dim isn't always a light you want to dim. The hallway, the stairs: on and off, full, every time, even on dimmable bulbs.

The setup treats the two as one. The dim test decides it, and the only way past that is the end page's row "The bulbs: Dim | On and off only" -- which reads as a fact about the bulbs, so it doesn't look like a choice, and picking On and off only there writes down something untrue about them.

And once setup is closed there is nowhere to change it. The end page says "Change any of it here, or later from the light", but no light's screen has the switch's settings: that sentence promises a place that doesn't exist.

TODAY -- FROM THE SHIPPED PANEL

Screenshots of the running panel against the mock house at 1440x900. The end page is app/src/SwitchSetup.vue's last step after a switch whose light dimmed. The light's screen is app/src/panes/LightPane.vue, the same screen a wall switch's light opens on (held open on the floor lamp here). Neither changes dimming after setup.

A -- ONE CHOICE, WHAT WAS FOUND UNDER IT

The end page's row becomes "From the switch: Dim | On and off only", and the small line under it says what the house found ("Its bulbs can dim" / "can't dim", "you saw it"). It starts at what was found; On and off only can always be picked; Dim can't be picked when the bulbs can't dim, and the line says why.

The light's screen gets one line about its switch, in the gap above the room's routine -- "Wall switch · dims · comes on when someone walks in" -- and Change opens the same page setup ended on, so there is one place the switch is set up, reached two ways. A change that needs the switch restarted says so there, as the end page does.

Cost: changing dimming later is two taps rather than one. That's right for something changed once a year.

RECOMMENDED: A

One row, worded as the choice it is, with the fact kept in small type where it explains rather than competes. And one place the switch's settings live, reached from setup's end and from the light, rather than two different controls that have to be kept in step. B shows the same information twice on the end page and puts a control on the light's screen that is touched almost never, beside ones touched every day. C asks every household with dimmable bulbs a question most of them answer the same way.

B -- TWO ROWS: FOUND, AND CHOSEN

The end page writes the fact down as its own row ("The bulbs: Can dim") and asks the choice in another ("The switch: Dims | Only turns it on and off"). The light's screen carries the choice itself, a segmented control in the gap above the room's routine, changed in place.

Cost: a row that only states a fact, on a page of things to change; and a control on the light's screen for something set once, next to the ones used every day -- the kind of thing that gets flipped by a stray tap.

C -- ASKED AS YOU GO

Right after a light dims smoothly, the same step asks "Should the switch dim it?" -- yes, dim it from the switch, or no, just on and off -- with the hallway and stairs as the examples. Bulbs that can't dim are never asked. The end page and the light's screen are A's.

Cost: one more question for every dimmable light, and most will answer yes. The setup's rule was that the house asks only what it can't find out; this is a preference, and a default with a way to change it serves it with no extra step.
